tldr: Without using any mechanical elastic energy storage like springs, an electrically actuated direct-drive jumping robot achieves a record jump height of 7.6 m and exceptional agility, driven by a long ~1.87 m leg and a novel fabric-wrap transmission.
hero_caption: Composite time-lapse of a vertical jump compared with a 1.83 m tall human. The robot leaps vigorously from the ground, reaching an apex of around 7.6 m—equivalent to the second or third floor of a building.
overview:
For high-jumping robots, the standard approach has long been parallel-elastic actuation: slowly storing energy in powerful springs and releasing it suddenly via clutches or latches. However, this approach adds parts and mass. It also requires winding times ranging from seconds to minutes before the next leap, making quick, repeated hopping difficult. In contrast, direct-drive (DD) systems connect the motor directly to the leg, enabling fast stance times and agile movements. Yet because jump height depends directly on the motor's instantaneous power, jumping high has remained a major challenge.

To overcome this, the authors turned to the scaling laws of direct-drive jumping: jump height scales with leg stroke length and power-to-weight ratio. Instead of using springs, they envisioned jumping using an extremely long single leg powered by a lightweight, high-power motor. However, lengthening the leg makes it prone to buckling and vibrations, and an efficient mechanism is needed to extract peak power across the motor's changing speed. Their answer is the "fabric-wrap transmission," which spools composite fabric tape around a pulley. As the tape wraps and builds up thickness, the mechanical advantage changes continuously. This keeps the motor operating near its peak power through the stroke without additional gears, while simultaneously bracing the slender leg against buckling.

Outdoor experiments with a 281 g robot validated a takeoff stance time of just 190 ms, reaching a jump height of 7.6 m—the highest yet reported for an electrically actuated, spring-free jumping robot—alongside top-tier jumping agility (5.30 m/s). Furthermore, small propellers at the top of the leg leverage the long moment arm to stabilize the upright balance on the ground and enable directed, tilted jumps.
contributions: Demonstrated a jump height of 7.6 m with a stance time of 190 ms on physical hardware, setting the highest record for an electrically actuated, spring-free direct-drive jumping robot.

Proposed and developed a fabric-wrap transmission that provides continuous variable mechanical advantage without extra gearing, maintaining near-peak motor power while bracing the slender leg against buckling.
Achieved ground balance and jump attitude control (including tilted jumps) using compact, low-thrust propeller thrusters that leverage the long leg's large lever arm.

sections.heading: Ditching springs for an ultra-long leg: A fresh take on jumping
sections.summary: This section reviews jump performance metrics and conventional actuation methods (series-elastic, parallel-elastic, and direct-drive), explaining how scaling direct-drive leg stroke to extremes yields unprecedented jump height without springs.
sections.details:
### I-A Motivation: The appeal of jumping and performance metrics
Jumping offers a powerful mode of locomotion for traversing rubble, rough terrain, or high ledges, as well as crater exploration in planetary missions. This paper evaluates jumping performance using jump height ($h$), jump frequency ($f_j = 1/(t_s + t_f)$, where $t_s$ is stance time and $t_f$ is flight time to apex), and their product: vertical jumping agility ($h \cdot f_j$). Agility measures how fast a robot can climb a series of vertical steps per unit time.

### I-B Contribution: Key contributions of this work
Unlike conventional high-jumping robots that store energy in springs, the authors propose a novel monopedal robot driven by a direct-drive (or quasi-direct-drive) setup over a long leg stroke. Using a specialized transmission with fabric tape, the robot achieves a jump height of 7.6 m—the highest ever reported for a spring-free electric robot.

### I-C Jumping Actuation Methods: Trade-offs among three paradigms
Actuation strategies for jumping robots fall into three main categories:
- Series-elastic: Springs are placed between the motor and the leg. They boost peak power and buffer impacts, but add mechanical complexity and lengthen stance time.
- Parallel-elastic: Motors slowly wind up springs through high gear ratios, releasing them via latches. This method holds the absolute jump height records (such as 32 m by Hawkes et al.), but recharging takes tens of seconds to minutes, limiting continuous jumping.
- Direct-drive (DD): Motors drive the leg directly (or via low-backlash, small-ratio gearing) without springs. Ignoring air resistance, jump height $h$ theoretically scales with maximum power $P_{\max}$, leg stroke $l_{\text{leg}}$, and total mass $M$ as $h \propto (P_{\max} / M)^{2/3} \, l_{\text{leg}}^{2/3}$. In other words, without adding springs, jumping high is entirely possible by maximizing the power-to-weight ratio and leg stroke length. This approach also yields a lightweight, simple structure, eliminates pre-jump charging delays, and provides superior controllability because ground reaction forces can be estimated directly from motor currents.

### I-D Related Works: Comparisons with existing jumping robots
The authors compare their work to series-elastic designs like Salto-1P, parallel-elastic designs like Hawkes et al., quadrupedal DD robots like Stanford Doggo and Minitaur, and monopedal cable-driven or rack-and-pinion robots like RAMIEL. Prior DD robots had short leg strokes and higher mass, keeping jump heights near ~1 m. This work breaks through that barrier by pushing the monopedal design to an ultralight, long-stroke extreme.

sections.heading: Spooling fabric to leap: The fabric-wrap transmission and attitude control
sections.summary: This section details the design of the ~2 m tall, 281 g robot. It introduces the mathematical model of the fabric-wrap transmission that creates a variable mechanical advantage as fabric spools onto a pulley, along with ground and flight attitude control via tip propellers.
sections.details:
### II-A System Overview: Three ultralight subsystems
The robot has a total mass of only 281 g and consists of three main subsystems:
- Leg: An ultralight carbon fiber tube (OD 6 mm, ID 5 mm, length 1981 mm, mass just 27 g). While light, it readily flexes on its own.
- Body (192 g): Located at the bottom of the leg, housing a Vertiq brushless DC motor (23-06, 2200 Kv), a 6S LiPo battery (550 mAh), an ESP32 microcontroller, and a landing tripod.
- Balancing Module (55 g): Mounted at the very top of the leg, carrying four coreless-motor-driven propellers, an IMU, and a 1S LiPo battery. Placing heavy components at the extremes keeps the center of mass close to the leg axis.

### II-B The Fabric-Wrap Transmission: Variable mechanical advantage and buckling brace
The core innovation is a high-strength Dyneema® composite fabric tape (width 6 mm, thickness 0.13 mm) wrapped helically around the leg at angle $\phi$ and spooled onto the motor shaft.
- Variable Mechanical Advantage: As the tape wraps around the spool, the spool radius $r(x)$ grows thicker. With initial radius $r_0$, tape thickness $t$, and leg extension $x$, the radius increases as $r(x) = \sqrt{r_0^2 + (t \cdot x) / (\pi \cos\phi)}$. Consequently, the mechanical advantage $\mathrm{MA} = \dot{\theta}/\dot{x} = 1/(r(x)\cos\phi)$ starts high (delivering high thrust) and decreases as the leg extends (favoring high velocity). Unlike fixed-gear drives (e.g., rack-and-pinion) that pass through motor speed regimes too quickly, this design keeps the motor in its current-limited peak power regime throughout most of the stroke.
- Buckling prevention: Tension in the helically wound tape provides an external bracing effect, preventing the long, thin carbon tube from buckling under jumping forces.
- Parameter optimization: Simulations identified practical optimal values: initial radius $r_0 = 2.0\text{ mm}$, thickness $t = 0.13\text{ mm}$, and wrap angle $\phi = 2.5^\circ$.

### II-C The Balancing Module: Leveraging the long leg for propeller control
Because the leg is nearly 2 m long, even small tip propellers enjoy a huge moment arm. Four thrusters (totaling ~0.50 N of thrust, only ~18% of robot weight) supply ample control torque.
- On the ground: Modeled as an inverted pendulum pivoting on the foot, stabilized to commanded angles (up to 15° tilt) using a gravity-compensated PD controller.
- In flight: Once airborne, rotation occurs about the center of mass. Upon detecting liftoff, gains instantly switch to flight mode for attitude stabilization.

### II-D Experiment Setup: Outdoor testing setup
In an outdoor grassy field, two high-speed cameras (GoPro HERO13 Black at 120 fps) performed stereo triangulation to accurately capture the 3D trajectory of the robot in flight.

sections.heading: Reaching 7.6 m: Real-world jump performance and tilted takeoff
sections.summary: Outdoor vertical jump trials confirmed a 7.6 m jump height (~2.5 s flight time), with telemetry verifying that the motor maintained near-peak power throughout the stroke. Ground tilt balancing and unassisted angled jumps were also successfully demonstrated.
sections.details:
### III-A Jump Height: A record-breaking 7.6 m spring-free electric jump
3D tracking analysis of vertical jump trials confirmed an apex displacement (jump height $\Delta Z$) of approximately 7.6 m. Total air time was roughly 2.5 s, and horizontal drift stayed within 1.6 m. Jumping agility reached 5.30 m/s—among the highest recorded for any electrically actuated jumping robot.
Motor telemetry (current and speed) showed that after initial spin-up, power output plateaued near peak capacity across the majority of the stroke, validating the variable mechanical advantage of the fabric-wrap transmission.

### III-B Attitude Control: Rejecting wind and holding commanded angles on the ground
Ground balancing trials proved the system could reject disturbances like outdoor wind to hold vertical, while also tracking step inputs in roll and pitch up to 15°. Attitude mode switching at takeoff was also demonstrated, though in-flight attitude convergence faced limitations as the body moved toward the tip, bringing the center of mass closer to the thrusters and shortening the moment arm.

### III-C Tilted Jump: A first step toward directional hopping
The robot also executed "tilted jumps," where propellers leaned the body by ~20° on the ground before triggering the jump command. The robot launched diagonally forward in just ~190 ms from the jump command. This marks a critical milestone toward directional multi-hopping over obstacles.

sections.heading: Takeaways and next steps: Toward continuous hopping and lunar exploration
sections.summary: The effectiveness of a long-stroke direct drive and fabric-wrap transmission is demonstrated with a 7.6 m jump height and 5.30 m/s agility. Future work focuses on in-flight body reset for continuous hopping and potential exploration missions on low-gravity worlds.
sections.details:
### Summary
By pairing high-power direct drive with an ultralight, long-stroke leg, this study achieved an unprecedented 7.6 m jump height for a spring-free electric robot. It also achieved a vertical jumping agility of 5.30 m/s—the highest among all electric jumping robots—proving the feasibility of jumping both high and fast.

### Future Challenges and Applications
- Realizing continuous hopping: This study demonstrated single jumps. Transitioning into subsequent jumps upon landing will require an in-flight retraction mechanism to quickly return the body to the base of the leg, alongside mid-air control.
- Applications of the mechanism: The fabric-wrap transmission, capable of rapid acceleration by spooling fabric, can be applied to lightweight, high-velocity catapult launchers for fixed-wing UAVs.
- Low-gravity exploration (Moon and asteroids): In reduced gravity, jump heights could reach tens of meters. This offers an exciting robotic locomotion concept capable of leaping over steep crater rims inaccessible to wheeled rovers, or surveying terrain from above like a drone in airless environments.

takeaways: Breaks the assumption that extreme jumps require strong springs; pushing scaling laws with long strokes and high-power direct drive can deliver jumps exceeding 7 m.

The fabric-wrap transmission leverages spool thickening to achieve variable mechanical advantage (sustaining peak motor power) while bracing slender rods against buckling—an exceptionally elegant mechanical solution without extra gears.
Capitalizing on the ultra-long monopedal leg provides an expansive lever arm, enabling miniature propeller thrusters to generate sufficient torque for ground balancing and tilt control.
limitations: Currently demonstrated only for single jumps; lacks an in-flight retraction mechanism and control strategy to reset the body for continuous landing and hopping.

At stroke completion, the body reaches the balancing module at the tip, shifting the center of mass close to the thrusters, drastically reducing the control moment arm and hindering flight attitude convergence.
The nearly 2 m rigid monopedal structure is impractical for indoor or low-ceiling environments, posing challenges for transportability and compact storage.
